questions.q: Why does Driftwood's architecture use two separate Snowflake warehouses instead of one shared warehouse?
options: So transformation (ETL) and reporting (BI) workloads don't queue behind each other, and each workload's cost and auto-suspend can be tuned and tracked independently
Because Snowflake requires a separate warehouse for every schema
Because dbt cannot run on the same warehouse as Power BI for technical reasons
To make the architecture diagram look more complex
questions.explain: Separating ETL and BI workloads onto their own warehouses means each can be sized and auto-suspended independently, and the bill can show which workload actually costs what.

questions.q: What is the point of the `driftwood` resource-naming convention, according to this lesson?
options: So every object in a shared account is identifiable as part of this project at a glance -- not about the specific word "driftwood" itself
Snowflake requires all object names to share a common prefix
It's purely for branding purposes with no practical benefit
To make object names as short as possible
questions.explain: The naming convention's value is recognizability in a shared account, not the specific prefix word chosen -- the same principle used in the AWS Capstone course's own naming table.

questions.q: Where does raw billing and usage data land before being loaded into Snowflake tables?
options: An internal Snowflake stage (@driftwood_raw_stage)
Directly into the marts schema
A local file on the Airflow server, never touching Snowflake
Power BI's own internal storage
questions.explain: Files land in the internal stage first, then get loaded into raw tables via COPY INTO -- the standard Snowflake ingestion pattern.

questions.q: What orchestrates the full daily sequence (load, transform, test)?
options: An Airflow DAG
A Power BI scheduled refresh alone
A human manually running each step
Snowflake Tasks exclusively, with no Airflow involvement
questions.explain: The Airflow DAG (driftwood_daily_elt) runs the full daily sequence; Power BI's own scheduled refresh picks up the result afterward, but doesn't orchestrate the upstream steps.

questions.q: Why do Snowflake database, schema, table, and warehouse names in this convention use underscores instead of the hyphens used elsewhere (like the Git repo name)?
options: Snowflake's own object-naming rules don't allow hyphens in those identifiers
Underscores are purely a stylistic preference with no technical reason
Hyphens are reserved for Airflow DAG IDs only
It's a typo that should be fixed to use hyphens everywhere
questions.explain: The naming table splits deliberately by what each service's identifier rules actually allow -- Snowflake objects require underscores, while Git repos and similar can use hyphens.
